item.title: Arashiyama Monkey Park: Wild Macaques and a City View — Guide
item.description: The Iwatayama Monkey Park sits on a hilltop above the Arashiyama district, home to a troop of more than a hundred wild Japanese macaques who roam freely across the open summit. Unlike a zoo, here the monkeys are unpenned and the visitors are the ones enclosed: you can buy food and hand it to the macaques through the mesh of a feeding hut, watching them up close while they stay wild and free outside.

item.title: Tenryuji: Arashiyama's Great Zen Temple and Borrowed-Scenery Garden — Guide
item.description: Tenryuji is the most important temple in Arashiyama and one of Kyoto’s five great Zen temples, founded in 1339. While its wooden halls have burned and been rebuilt many times, its garden survives from the fourteenth century essentially unchanged — a masterpiece by the monk-designer Muso Soseki. Centred on a pond, it uses the technique of shakkei, ‘borrowed scenery’, drawing the wooded slopes of the Arashiyama hills into the composition so that garden and mountain read as one.

item.title: Arashiyama Guide: Bamboo Grove, Temples & the Hozu River
item.description: On the western edge of Kyoto, where the city meets forested mountains and the Hozu River, lies Arashiyama — a district that packs a soaring bamboo grove, a UNESCO Zen garden, a monkey mountain, riverboats, a scenic railway, and a famous moon-crossing bridge into one beautiful, walkable area. The towering green corridor of the bamboo grove is the headline image, but Arashiyama rewards a full half-day or more of exploring.

item.title: Kyoto Autumn Foliage Guide: The Best Momiji Spots & Timing
item.description: Autumn may be Kyoto at its most beautiful. For a few magical weeks each November, the city’s maples (momiji) turn fiery red, orange, and gold, setting temple halls, gardens, hillsides, and rivers ablaze with colour. The Japanese love of koyo (autumn leaves) rivals their devotion to cherry blossom, and Kyoto — with its hundreds of temples framed by maples — is the country’s premier destination to enjoy it. This guide covers when the foliage peaks, the very best places to see it, the spectacular night illuminations, and how to plan around the considerable crowds.

item.title: Sagano Scenic Railway Guide: The Romantic Train Through the Gorge
item.description: The Sagano Romantic Train, known affectionately as the Torokko, is a nostalgic open-window sightseeing train that trundles along the cliffs of the Hozu River gorge between Arashiyama and Kameoka. For 25 slow, scenic minutes it follows the river through forested mountains that explode with colour in autumn, froth with cherry blossom in spring, and glow deep green in summer — a beloved Kyoto experience that pairs perfectly with a traditional boat ride back down the same gorge.

item.title: Kyoto Nature: Bamboo Groves, Mountain Hikes & Seasonal Gardens
item.description: Kyoto’s nature is inseparable from its culture — the city’s temples and shrines were built to frame specific views of mountains, rivers, and seasonal trees. Cherry blossoms at the Philosopher’s Path, autumn maples at Jojakko-ji, moss gardens at Saihoji, cedar forest at Fushimi Inari — each experience is both natural and profoundly designed. This guide covers Kyoto’s finest nature experiences, with the practical timing that makes the difference between the experience and a photograph of the experience.

item.title: Kyoto Sightseeing: Top 25 Temples, Shrines & Unmissable Spots
item.description: Kyoto contains 17 UNESCO World Heritage sites, over 1,600 Buddhist temples, and more than 400 Shinto shrines — the highest density of designated cultural properties in Japan. This guide selects the 25 essential experiences, organises them by district, and provides the specific timing and access information that separates a memorable visit from a crowded one. ⛩️ Fushimi Inari Taisha — The Thousand Torii Gates District: Fushimi | Access: Inari Station (JR Nara Line, 5 min from Kyoto Station) — station exit opens directly to shrine gate Admission: Free | Open: 24 hours
